title: Advantages and disadvantages of the market system

blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the market economic system, with examples from different countries, and weigh the two sides for named groups.

blocks.heading: How the machinery produces its advantages
blocks.text: Prices act as signals and incentives. When mangoes at the Oshakati open market are scarce after a poor harvest, the price rises; the higher price tells buyers to take less and tells any farmer with fruit that bringing it is now worth the trip, so resources move to the good people want most. The same chain drives consumer sovereignty: Kaoko Juice earns revenue where buyers spend, so it tends to produce the flavours buyers choose. Competition adds a third advantage: a seller charging far above its rivals tends to lose sales, so rivalry holds prices down and choice wide. Together the profit motive and prices move resources to their most valued uses without a central plan. Vietnam's farm markets after its 1980s reforms show the same chains at work.

blocks.heading: Where the machinery misfires
blocks.text: The market system also misfires. Income is distributed unevenly, because rewards follow scarce skills and ownership: a household owning two taxis earns far more than a security guard. Street lighting in Katutura tends to be under-provided, because a firm cannot charge each person who benefits from the glow. Goods that impose costs on others may still be produced where the profit is good: a plant releasing waste into a river keeps the sales while people downstream carry the harm. And work is not guaranteed, because firms hire for expected profit, not for the need for jobs.

blocks.heading: Weighing the two sides
blocks.text: The judgement depends on the good and the group. For consumer goods - juice, clothing, haircuts - the market's advantages dominate: choice is wide, rivalry holds prices down, resources follow what buyers value. For goods that spread their benefits beyond the buyer, or for households with no resources to sell, the disadvantages bite hardest. The weighing ends with a condition: the market serves consumers well where goods can be sold one-by-one and rivalry is real. Topic 2.11 shows the compromise most countries adopt.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The misfires named here are gathered up as market failure in topic 2.10; the responses a government can make belong to topic 2.11; the rivalry that holds prices down reappears in topic 3.8.
